passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel emerged in common-law jurisdictions as a judicial remedy for a persistent gap in classical contract theory: the rule that a promise unsupported by consideration — that is, by some exchange of value — is ordinarily unenforceable. Classical doctrine thus left promisees who had detrimentally relied on gratuitous assurances without legal recourse, a result that many jurists regarded as unjust. Promissory estoppel addresses this gap by allowing a court to enforce a promise when the promisee has reasonably relied on it to his or her detriment, even in the absence of a bargained-for exchange. The doctrine's apparent simplicity, however, masks deep disagreements about its proper scope and justification.

Two competing theoretical accounts of promissory estoppel generate different conclusions about its reach. Under the reliance-based account, the doctrine's purpose is compensatory: the promisee is entitled to recover precisely the losses flowing from reasonable reliance, but no more. A court following this view would therefore limit recovery to the promisee's out-of-pocket expenses, declining to award the "expectation interest" — the benefit the promisee would have obtained had the promise been fulfilled. The alternative, obligations-based account holds that promissory estoppel merely supplements, rather than displaces, classical contract law; under this view, once the conditions for estoppel are met, a court may award full expectation damages equivalent to those available in a breach-of-contract action. Courts in England and Australia have, on the whole, favored the reliance-based view, while many courts in the United States have gradually moved toward the obligations-based approach, particularly following the broad formulation adopted in the second Restatement of Contracts in 1981.

The divergence in outcomes produced by these two accounts is illustrated clearly by cases in which a supplier makes an unambiguous promise to deliver goods at a fixed price, inducing a manufacturer to plan an entire production run, only for the supplier to withdraw the promise before any formal contract is concluded. Under the reliance-based account, the manufacturer could recover only the wasted planning costs already incurred. Under the obligations-based account, the manufacturer would recover the full profits it expected to earn from the production run. The stakes of the theoretical choice are therefore substantial, and critics of the obligations-based approach have argued that permitting full expectation recovery via estoppel effectively circumvents the consideration requirement, reducing the significance of the formal contract to a procedural formality. This criticism has considerable force; it would be unfortunate if the doctrine were extended so far as to dissolve the line between the enforceability of a bare promise and that of a bargained-for contract. One hopes that courts will continue to calibrate estoppel awards to the actual detriment suffered by the promisee, reserving full expectation recovery for those cases in which the reliance and the expected benefit are, as a practical matter, indistinguishable.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was created to prevent unjust outcomes in cases where formal contracts were improperly drafted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reliance-based account of promissory estoppel is superior to the obligations-based account and should be universally adopted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel fills a gap in classical contract law, but competing theoretical accounts of the doctrine produce different and potentially problematic outcomes, and the proper scope of the doctrine remains disputed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in England and Australia have more faithfully applied classical contract doctrine than courts in the United States because they prefer the reliance-based account of promissory estoppel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel should be abolished because it effectively renders the consideration requirement obsolete.

explanations.correct: The passage spans the origin and purpose of promissory estoppel, the two competing theoretical accounts, their divergent outcomes, and the author's cautionary editorial at the close. C integrates all of these strands without overstating the author's conclusion.
explanations.A: Too narrow and inaccurate — the passage identifies gratuitous, unsupported promises as the gap, not improperly drafted contracts.
explanations.B: Overstates the author's position — the author urges restraint in awarding expectation damages but does not endorse full universal adoption of the reliance-based account.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement of one descriptive claim; the passage's main concern is the theoretical debate, not a comparison of national judiciaries.
explanations.E: Reverses the author's stance — the author warns against extending estoppel too far but does not advocate abolition of the doctrine.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the obligations-based account of promissory estoppel can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, because it provides promisees with full compensation for their losses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified concern, because unrestricted application of the account risks undermining the significance of formal contract requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: complete indifference, as the author considers both theoretical accounts equally valid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: unambiguous hostility, because the account was improperly formulated in the second Restatement of Contracts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious approval of its application in English and Australian courts but skepticism about its use in the United States.

explanations.correct: The author acknowledges the criticism of the obligations-based account has 'considerable force' and warns that extending estoppel to dissolve the line between bare promises and bargained contracts would be 'unfortunate,' signaling qualified concern rather than hostility or endorsement.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity — the author's closing paragraph expresses worry about the approach's extension, not enthusiasm.
explanations.C: Wrong valence — the author clearly takes a position, preferring calibrated reliance-based recovery over full expectation awards.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author never attacks the Restatement's formulation as improper; the concern is about courts extending the doctrine too far.
explanations.E: Inverts the passage's geographic claims — it is English and Australian courts that favor the reliance-based view, not the obligations-based one.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its historical origins explained; two competing theoretical accounts of the doctrine are contrasted; an illustrative case is presented to show the accounts' divergent outcomes; and the author offers a cautionary assessment favoring limited application of the doctrine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal rule is described; one court's application of the rule is criticized; an alternative rule is proposed; and the author endorses the alternative rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shortcomings of classical contract law are enumerated; a statutory remedy for those shortcomings is analyzed; and the author concludes that the statute has fully resolved the problem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two legal doctrines are defined and compared; their respective historical origins are traced; and the author concludes that one jurisdiction has more successfully implemented the doctrines than others.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A gap in classical contract law is identified; one judicial response to that gap is examined in detail; and the author concludes that the gap should be addressed through legislative reform rather than judicial innovation.

explanations.correct: A precisely mirrors the passage's four-paragraph movement: introduction of promissory estoppel and the gap it fills (paragraph 1), contrast of the two accounts (paragraph 2), the supplier-manufacturer illustration (paragraph 3), and the author's cautionary closing editorial (paragraph 3's final sentences).
explanations.B: Mis-sequences — the passage contrasts two theoretical accounts rather than criticizing a specific court's application and proposing an alternative rule.
explanations.C: Inaccurate on two counts — promissory estoppel is a common-law doctrine, not a statute, and the author does not conclude the problem is fully resolved.
explanations.D: Wrong grain — the passage describes one doctrine (promissory estoppel) with two accounts, not two distinct doctrines, and does not conclude that one jurisdiction has 'more successfully' implemented them.
explanations.E: Plausible but unused move — the author nowhere calls for legislative reform; the closing sentence addresses courts directly.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following most accurately describes the "expectation interest" as that term is used in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee's out-of-pocket expenses incurred in reasonable reliance on the promise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The benefit the promisee would have obtained had the promise been performed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The amount necessary to restore the promisee to the position held before the promise was made.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The consideration that would have been exchanged had a formal contract been concluded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The damages available when a court determines that a promisee's reliance was unreasonable.

explanations.correct: The passage states the expectation interest is 'the benefit the promisee would have obtained had the promise been fulfilled,' directly defining the term in paragraph 2.
explanations.A: This describes the reliance interest — what the reliance-based account would award — not the expectation interest.
explanations.C: This describes a restitutionary or status-quo-ante measure, which the passage does not associate with the expectation interest.
explanations.D: This introduces the concept of consideration, which the passage associates with formal contracts, not with the expectation interest per se.
explanations.E: Altered qualifier — the passage says promissory estoppel applies when reliance is reasonable, not unreasonable; this choice inverts the doctrine's conditions.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should never be used to award damages exceeding a promisee's actual out-of-pocket losses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be abolished in all common-law contract cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In some circumstances, a court applying promissory estoppel may appropriately award full expectation damages when the promisee's reliance losses and expected benefit are practically indistinguishable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second Restatement of Contracts was a mistake because it encouraged courts to expand estoppel beyond its original scope.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts in the United States should adopt the approach used by English and Australian courts in all cases involving promissory estoppel.

explanations.correct: The author's closing sentence explicitly reserves full expectation recovery for cases in which reliance and expected benefit are 'as a practical matter, indistinguishable,' supporting C as an inference the author would endorse.
explanations.A: Too absolute — the author's own closing sentence carves out an exception when reliance losses and expectation are indistinguishable, so 'never' overstates the author's position.
explanations.B: Outside scope and too strong — the author never argues for abolishing consideration; the concern is only about over-extending estoppel.
explanations.D: The passage does not criticize the Restatement itself; the concern is about courts extending the doctrine too far, not about the Restatement being mistaken.
explanations.E: Overstates — the author does not call for wholesale adoption of the English-Australian approach; the closing sentence is more nuanced, asking courts to calibrate awards to actual detriment.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the supplier-manufacturer scenario in the third paragraph in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate concretely how the two competing theoretical accounts yield significantly different damages outcomes in the same factual situation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that suppliers are more often at fault than manufacturers in commercial disputes involving unexecuted promises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide an example of a case in which the consideration requirement was satisfied despite the absence of a signed contract.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that the obligations-based account has been universally adopted in cases involving commercial supply chains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a new theoretical framework for resolving disputes between suppliers and manufacturers.

explanations.correct: The paragraph explicitly sets up the scenario to apply both accounts in turn — reliance-based yields only wasted planning costs; obligations-based yields full lost profits — making concrete the abstract theoretical divergence discussed in paragraph 2.
explanations.B: Accurate content, wrong function — the scenario involves a supplier's withdrawal but the purpose is doctrinal illustration, not fault assignment.
explanations.C: Inverts the scenario's logic — the whole point is that no formal contract was concluded and there was no consideration; the scenario is about the absence of those elements.
explanations.D: Overstates and wrong direction — the author presents the scenario to show a contested outcome, not to assert universal adoption.
explanations.E: Plausible but unused move — the author applies existing accounts to the scenario and offers no new theoretical framework.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the criticism of the obligations-based account described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many commercial actors never bother to formalize their agreements in written contracts even when they intend to be legally bound.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Empirical studies show that awarding full expectation damages under promissory estoppel does not measurably reduce the frequency with which parties conclude formal, consideration-supported contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several courts applying the reliance-based account have awarded damages that exceeded the promisee's documented out-of-pocket costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second Restatement of Contracts was drafted by a committee that included prominent critics of classical contract doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In jurisdictions that apply the obligations-based account, promissory estoppel claims are filed far more frequently than breach-of-contract claims.

explanations.correct: The criticism is that the obligations-based account 'effectively circumvents the consideration requirement' and risks dissolving the line between bare promises and formal contracts. If empirical evidence shows that full expectation awards do not in fact reduce parties' motivation to conclude formal contracts, the practical force of this concern is directly undermined.
explanations.A: This is tangential — the fact that parties sometimes forgo formality does not address whether estoppel awards erode the doctrinal significance of formal contracts.
explanations.C: This weakens the reliance-based account's internal consistency rather than the criticism directed at the obligations-based account; it targets a different claim.
explanations.D: The composition of the Restatement drafting committee is irrelevant to whether the obligations-based account undermines the consideration requirement in practice.
explanations.E: This would, if anything, support the criticism by suggesting the obligations-based approach is displacing formal contract claims — the opposite of undermining the criticism.
